source: Simon (1962) The architecture of complexity (Proc. Am. Philos. Soc. 106(6):467-482)
finding: Simon's Hora and Tempus parable is the founding quantitative case for decomposing a hard task into stable sub-assemblies. Both makers build a 1,000-part watch and are interrupted at random. Tempus must restart from zero after each interruption. Hora builds 10-part subassemblies, so an interruption costs little.
numbers: Interruption chance 1 in 100 per part added. Tempus finishes an uninterrupted watch with probability 0.99^1000, about 44 in a million attempts. Hora finishes a 10-part unit about 9 times in 10. Net ratio: Tempus needs about 4,000 times as long (1/111 x 20 x 20,000).
quote: Tempus will complete an assembly only 44 times per million attempts
limits: Illustrative model with assumed numbers, not an experiment. Assumes sub-assemblies are stable and independent, which is exactly what is hard to guarantee in a real design.
agent_relevance: Core argument for O3 Decompose: the gain comes from stable intermediate results that survive an interruption or an error, not from splitting alone. Each sub-answer must be checked and kept so a later failure does not erase it.

source: Simon (1962) The architecture of complexity (Proc. Am. Philos. Soc. 106(6):467-482)
finding: The clicking-safe example shows why decomposition cuts search from impossible to trivial: when each dial gives feedback on its own, dials can be set independently.
numbers: Ten dials, 100 settings each. Blind search: 100^10 settings, about 50 billion billion tries on average. With a click per correct dial: about 10 x 50 = 500 tries.
limits: The gain needs independent, separately checkable feedback per part. Without a per-part signal the search stays exponential.
agent_relevance: For O3, a decomposition only helps if code can test each sub-problem alone. A sub-problem with no separate check gives no savings. This supports the SUBFIELDS question: can parts be checked on their own.

source: Simon (1962) The architecture of complexity (Proc. Am. Philos. Soc. 106(6):467-482)
finding: Simon defines near-decomposability. Links inside a component are stronger than links between components, so short-run behaviour of each part is roughly independent of the others and long-run behaviour depends only on aggregates of the others.
numbers: Two properties: (a) short-run independence of components; (b) in the long run a component depends on the others only in an aggregate way. No experiment.
limits: Descriptive claim about physical, biological and social systems. It does not give a test for how decomposable a given problem is.
agent_relevance: Gives a plain test for O3: split where cross-links are weak. If the sub-problems need each other's detail, the split is bad and should be dropped.

source: Simon (1962) The architecture of complexity (Proc. Am. Philos. Soc. 106(6):467-482)
finding: Simon argues hierarchy aids description and comprehension: people draw and describe complex objects in a hierarchic order, and systems that are not nearly decomposable may escape our understanding.
numbers: Example: drawing a face, outline first, then features, then details. Problem solving is framed as selective trial and error, where selectivity comes from structure.
limits: Argument from examples. The human drawing claim is cited from other work, not tested here.
agent_relevance: Supports giving the model a short outline of parts before detail. Does not show that an LLM gains from it.

source: Simon (1962) The architecture of complexity (Proc. Am. Philos. Soc. 106(6):467-482)
finding: Simon notes that in a nearly decomposable system the sub-parts can be treated in aggregate by the whole, so little information is lost by a hierarchic description. The loss is the weak cross-links.
numbers: Statement made for physical, social and economic examples including input-output economic matrices. No numeric loss bound is given.
limits: The loss from ignoring weak links is assumed small, not measured.
agent_relevance: The cost of O3 is the weak cross-links dropped. After solving parts, a combine step must restore them, and S-state checks should test the combined answer, not only the parts.

source: Parnas (1972) On the criteria to be used in decomposing systems into modules (CACM 15(12):1053-1058)
finding: Parnas compares two ways to split the same KWIC-index program. The first follows processing steps like a flowchart. The second hides one design decision per module. The split by processing step is the function-style decomposition. He judges the hiding style better on change, independent development and comprehension.
numbers: Same small program decomposed two ways. Criteria: changeability (he lists 5 likely-to-change design decisions that touch many modules in version 1), independent development, comprehensibility. No participant data.
quote: the criterion used was to make each major step in the processing a module
limits: Qualitative design argument. Parnas says his comprehension judgement is subjective. One toy system. Flowchart approach was said to suffice for systems of about 5,000-10,000 instructions.
agent_relevance: Key caveat for functional decomposition by flow of steps: it is simple but couples modules through shared data formats. For code tasks, split by decision to hide, not by step. For answer tasks, prefer parts with narrow, stated interfaces.

source: Parnas (1972) On the criteria to be used in decomposing systems into modules (CACM 15(12):1053-1058)
finding: In the flowchart decomposition the interfaces are complex table formats that must be fixed jointly. In the hiding decomposition the interfaces are function names and parameter types, so teams can start much earlier and in parallel.
numbers: Qualitative. Parnas lists five decisions (for example storing all lines in core, packing characters, building a shift index) that would force changes across many modules in version 1 but only one module in version 2.
limits: Claimed from analysis, not timed. Modern teams may weigh these costs differently.
agent_relevance: For O3, give each sub-problem a short written interface (inputs, output form) before solving. That is the cheap way to keep parts independent.

source: Parnas (1972) On the criteria to be used in decomposing systems into modules (CACM 15(12):1053-1058)
finding: Parnas warns that a decomposition can still leak: his own circular-shift module fixed the order of shifts, which revealed more than needed and limited later designs. He calls this a design error.
numbers: One worked example in the paper. No counts.
limits: Self-critique within a single example.
agent_relevance: When an LLM writes a sub-problem spec, over-specifying the form of the answer can block good solutions. Specify what must hold, not how.

source: Ulrich (1995) The role of product architecture in the manufacturing firm (Research Policy 24:419-440)
finding: Ulrich defines product architecture as the scheme that allocates function (a function structure of functional elements) to physical components, plus the interfaces between them. A modular architecture has a one-to-one map from functional elements to components and decoupled interfaces. An integral one has a complex map or coupled interfaces.
numbers: Typology links architecture to five areas: product change, product variety, component standardization, product performance, product development management. Trailer example: 6 functional elements, modular versus integral layouts.
limits: Conceptual synthesis, not an experiment. Examples are few and from hardware firms.
agent_relevance: Function-to-part mapping is the thing a decomposition tries to make one-to-one. When the model's sub-problems map one-to-one to checkable pieces, parts can be tested and changed alone. If not, expect coupled failures.

source: Ulrich (1995) The role of product architecture in the manufacturing firm (Research Policy 24:419-440)
finding: Ulrich notes that function structures at more detailed levels embed more assumptions about the working principle, so two products that do the same thing may have different function structures when described in detail.
numbers: Example: expand cargo capacity assumes nothing about towing, while the detailed trailer function structure of 6 elements assumes a road trailer.
limits: Illustration only.
agent_relevance: A decomposition made too early or too fine fixes the solution type. Decompose at the abstraction level that keeps the answer space open until the parts are chosen.

source: Stone and Wood (1999/2000) Development of a functional basis for design (DETC99/DTM-8765; J. Mech. Des. 122(4):359-370)
finding: Stone and Wood propose a controlled verb-object language for function: functions as operations on flows of material, energy and signal. It gives a fixed stopping level for decomposition and a common vocabulary for archiving and comparing products. The abstract page was read; the paper body was not available.
numbers: Reported later (Hirtz 2002): built from a review of over 30 articles from four continents and empirical study of over 100 products; 3 flow classes and 8 function classes.
limits: Only the abstract page and later secondary descriptions were read. Original numbers and examples such as the popcorn popper are taken from Vermaas 2007 and Hirtz 2002.
agent_relevance: Gives the model a closed list of verbs to describe sub-functions. Whether an LLM benefits from a closed verb list is untested here.

source: Hirtz, Stone, McAdams, Szykman, Wood (2002) A functional basis for engineering design: reconciling and evolving previous efforts (NIST TN 1447; Res. Eng. Des. 13(2):65-82)
finding: The functional basis is the vocabulary behind function-structure decomposition. Two independent efforts, a NIST taxonomy and the Stone and Wood basis, were merged. The lineage draws on value engineering from the 1940s, Pahl and Beitz, and TRIZ.
numbers: NIST taxonomy: over 130 functions and over 100 flows from a review of over 40 articles; 6 class functions. Stone and Wood basis: 8 class functions, 3 flow classes, built from over 100 products.
limits: The text says the name basis was chosen to borrow the mathematical qualities of spanning and independence; no test of those qualities is given.
agent_relevance: Shows a standard action vocabulary was a real engineering need, because free text led to ambiguity and many ways to model one design.

source: Hirtz, Stone, McAdams, Szykman, Wood (2002) A functional basis for engineering design: reconciling and evolving previous efforts (NIST TN 1447; Res. Eng. Des. 13(2):65-82)
finding: The reconciled basis has 3 flow classes (material, signal, energy) and 8 function classes: branch, channel, connect, control magnitude, convert, provision, signal, support. Terms sit at class, secondary and tertiary levels plus correspondents (synonym mapping).
numbers: Reconciled sets: 53 function terms and 42 flow terms. Energy class has 13 secondary categories; material 5; signal 2.
limits: The paper text calls the 8 groups secondary in one place; the tables show they are the class level.
agent_relevance: The correspondents idea is useful: map free words to a small set. A scaffold could map a model's sub-task wording to a few types.

source: Hirtz, Stone, McAdams, Szykman, Wood (2002) A functional basis for engineering design: reconciling and evolving previous efforts (NIST TN 1447; Res. Eng. Des. 13(2):65-82)
finding: Convergence check: the authors argue that if independent efforts land on similar term sets, a fundamental set may exist. Overlap was high.
numbers: Of 53 function terms: 46 appear in the NIST taxonomy and 47 in the original basis. Of 42 flow terms: 34 in NIST and 27 in the original basis; only 2 non-human flow terms were missing from NIST.
limits: Not independent in the strict sense: both efforts drew on Pahl and Beitz and overlapping literature. Overlap shows agreement, not that the set is complete or optimal.
agent_relevance: Agreement on a small action set is modest support that a few generic sub-function types suffice for hardware. It says nothing about reasoning tasks.

source: Hirtz, Stone, McAdams, Szykman, Wood (2002) A functional basis for engineering design: reconciling and evolving previous efforts (NIST TN 1447; Res. Eng. Des. 13(2):65-82)
finding: Validation in this report was by use, not by a controlled trial: NIST modelled power tools, a vacuum transport system and archive encasements; Ford used it in Design for Six Sigma. The report cites Kurfman et al. (2000) for a repeatability study.
numbers: No effect sizes. Ford reception described as great enthusiasm. Cited repeatability tests are in Kurfman et al. 2001/2003.
limits: Anecdotal evidence. The device-function view excludes the user, so human actions are modeled separately.
agent_relevance: There is no outcome evidence here that decomposing improves designs. Use as vocabulary evidence only.

source: Hirtz, Stone, McAdams, Szykman, Wood (2002) A functional basis for engineering design: reconciling and evolving previous efforts (NIST TN 1447; Res. Eng. Des. 13(2):65-82)
finding: The authors say functional modelling guides problem decomposition, physical modelling, product architecting, concept generation and team organization, but give no measurement that it does. They list reduced ambiguity and uniform information as the main justification.
numbers: Three reasons listed: less ambiguity, uniqueness at concept level, uniformity of information.
limits: Claims are design-theory arguments. Compare Booth et al. 2015 which found no link to design quality.
agent_relevance: Keep the benefit claims separate from the measured results in this subfield. Measured effect on quality is weak.

source: Vermaas (2007) The functional modelling account of Stone and Wood: some critical remarks (ICED'07 paper 140)
finding: Vermaas analyses the Stone and Wood account with conceptual tools. It holds two different notions of function: one as verb-object phrases, one as verbs only. It also claims the operations-on-flows description may really show behaviour, not intended function.
numbers: Popcorn popper example: initial model has corn, electricity, popcorn flows; final model adds melted butter, air, thermal and pneumatic energy flows. A cup hold liquid and retain heat breaks into 12 functional-basis subfunctions.
limits: Philosophical analysis with toy examples. No data. Author says critique does not affect the archiving claim.
agent_relevance: Warns that listing every flow gives behaviour, not purpose. The agent's decomposition should list only what the goal intends.

source: Vermaas (2007) The functional modelling account of Stone and Wood: some critical remarks (ICED'07 paper 140)
finding: Main criticism for design use: functional-basis subfunctions need not match small, easily solvable subfunctions. Some are too big to solve for a new technology, and some easy problems get split into many pieces.
numbers: Cup example needs 12 basis subfunctions though a cup is a single easy solution. Example of a hard basis subfunction: convert electrical energy to rotational energy, hard for motor designers.
quote: subfunctions defined in the account need not always coincide with subfunctions that can be taken as elementary in designing
limits: Context dependence argued by example only.
agent_relevance: This is the heart of O3: the right grain depends on what solutions the solver already has. Stop splitting when a sub-problem is solvable directly, and do not use a fixed grain.

source: Vermaas (2007) The functional modelling account of Stone and Wood: some critical remarks (ICED'07 paper 140)
finding: Vermaas examines the Concept Generator, which only keeps models whose subfunctions have stored solutions. It avoids unsolvable parts, but cannot recover when the repository lacks a solution for a cluster of basis functions.
numbers: Battery as a solution to provide electrical energy and stabilise needs stored behaviour such as mass density, not only stored functions.
limits: Argument about a particular algorithm; no test run.
agent_relevance: Decomposition checked against a solution library avoids dead-end parts, but a library gap hides good merged solutions.

source: Vermaas (2007) The functional modelling account of Stone and Wood: some critical remarks (ICED'07 paper 140)
finding: Proposed fixes: treat basis descriptions as behaviour, mark the designer-intended flows as the function, and keep a second, coarser decomposition into easily solvable parts.
numbers: Two-level proposal: one fine decomposition in basis terms and one coarse one in solvable parts.
limits: Proposal, untested.
agent_relevance: Two-layer idea fits the schema: a fine functional list for understanding, and a coarse set of 2 to 4 testable sub-problems for solving.

source: Kurfman, Stock, Stone, Rajan, Wood (2003) Experimental studies assessing the repeatability of a functional modeling derivation method (J. Mech. Des. 125(4):682-693)
finding: The only founding controlled test of Stone and Wood's method found: three experiments with designers of different skill, asking whether different people get the same functional model of a product using the derivation method. Authors report the method improves repeatability and leads toward a unique model.
numbers: Three experiments; the participant counts and agreement percentages could not be read (full text blocked by a bot check).
quote: Results indicate the method enhances repeatability
limits: Abstract page only; the paper body was not read. It tests agreement between modelers, not the quality of designs made from the models.
agent_relevance: Repeatability of a decomposition across solvers is a testable property. Our agent can check how often two runs give the same decomposition.

source: Kurfman, Stone, Rajan, Wood (2001) Functional modeling experimental studies (DETC2001, vol 4, pp 267-279)
finding: Conference version of the repeatability experiments. It frames the question as whether new design methods advance the field or only add theory, and calls the method largely successful, with named strengths and gaps.
numbers: Three experiments with participants of varying skill; numbers not available on the record page.
limits: PDF not available; abstract page only.
agent_relevance: Same as the 2003 entry: agreement across solvers is the measured outcome.

source: Caldwell, Sen, Mocko, Summers (2010/2011) An empirical study of the expressiveness of the functional basis (AI EDAM)
finding: A frequency study of how the functional basis is used in a web repository of consumer-product models. The tertiary level was judged too coarse to capture the detail modellers need, and flow terms need more expressiveness.
numbers: 121 models: 11 graphical function structures and 110 list-based models. Term-frequency counts were not on the page read.
quote: the tertiary terms are inappropriate for capturing sufficient details
limits: Abstract page only. One repository, reverse-engineered consumer products, same group that curates the repository.
agent_relevance: A fixed vocabulary can be too coarse at the finest level; allow free qualifiers on flows.

source: Sen, Caldwell, Summers, Mocko (2010) Evaluation of the functional basis using an information-theoretic approach (AI EDAM 24(1):87-105)
finding: A computational metric of information content for function models as graphs with verbs as nodes and objects as edges. Applied to repository models, the secondary level of the basis was most beneficial in information content and density.
numbers: No numbers on the page read. Conclusion: secondary level of the 3-level hierarchy is the best level.
limits: Abstract page only. Information content is not the same as usefulness to a designer. Same repository group.
agent_relevance: Gives a formal, countable measure of a decomposition's information. Could score an LLM decomposition for detail without judging it by eye.

source: Chandrasekaran (2005) Representing function: relating functional representation and functional modeling research streams (AI EDAM 19(2):65-74)
finding: Argues the two research streams are complementary: functional representation (FR) gives a formal device ontology for automated reasoning; functional modelling (FM) gives domain-specific behaviour primitives and catalogues. Function comes from need and from structure and component functions.
numbers: None.
limits: Abstract only. Position paper.
agent_relevance: Both views suggest a decomposition holds two things: the purpose, and a check that structure can deliver it.

source: van Eck (2009) On relating functional modeling approaches: abstracting functional models from behavioral models (ICED'09 paper 169)
finding: Surveys seven functional modelling approaches. In four (Multi Level Flow, Otto and Wood, Stone and Wood Functional Basis, Chakrabarti and Bligh) function is an input-output flow transformation. In three (Deng, Kitamura and Mizoguchi, Price et al.) function is an intended role of behaviour. Van Eck argues the flow kind equals behaviour and gives a two-step conversion that loses less than earlier methods.
numbers: 7 approaches compared; demonstration on a power screwdriver model in three frameworks.
limits: Method is analytic and example-based; the paper says empirical testing is left to others. One example product.
agent_relevance: There is no single agreed meaning of function. Our decomposition should fix its own meaning: sub-answer must serve the stated goal.

source: Gericke and Eisenbart (2017) The integrated function modeling framework and its relation to function structures (AI EDAM 31:436-457)
finding: A benchmark of function structures against the newer IFM framework on one glue gun, using criteria from Summers et al. (2013). The authors judge IFM more comprehensive and better for varied analyses. They also state that function structures are among the most widespread function modelling methods in research and practice.
numbers: One product (glue gun); two modellers who are also IFM authors; scores agreed by discussion until consensus.
limits: Authors developed IFM, so there is bias; they note their own impression may be biased. N is one product.
agent_relevance: Not evidence that one decomposition format is better for solving. It shows function-structure formats have no standard head-to-head tests.

source: Gericke and Eisenbart (2017) The integrated function modeling framework and its relation to function structures (AI EDAM 31:436-457)
finding: The paper says empirical evidence for the claimed benefits of function modelling in practice is only initial and cites Kurfman et al. 2001/2003, Caldwell et al. 2011, Srinivasan et al. 2012 and Sen et al. 2013 as the base.
numbers: Count of cited empirical studies: 4 groups. No effect sizes given in this paper.
limits: Literature statement by the authors, not a systematic review.
agent_relevance: Confirms the gap: as of 2017 the evidence that functional decomposition improves design is thin, matching the Purdue study.

source: Booth, Bhasin, Reid, Ramani (2015) Empirical studies of functional decomposition in early design (DETC2015-47865)
finding: Abstract page read to confirm the Purdue result (full text covered in evidence_b). Study 1: top-down and energy-flow decomposition similar, enumeration worse; Study 2: about half of 78 industry reports used decomposition with no link to design grade.
numbers: Study 1: 25 novice teams. Study 2: 78 industry-engineer reports. About half used decomposition; half of function diagrams tree-shaped.
limits: Abstract page only in this file; detail in evidence_b01 to b06.
agent_relevance: The best field evidence says decomposition helps communication and not directly quality. Keep expectations for O3 modest and measure it ourselves.

source: Erden, Komoto, van Beek, D'Amelio, Echavarria, Tomiyama (2008) A review of function modeling: approaches and applications (AI EDAM 22(2):147-169)
finding: Abstract page read. A comparative review of function modelling approaches and how they relate to AI, design theory and maintenance. Full text paywalled. Cited by later papers as showing a wealth of approaches with different function definitions.
numbers: A later paper reports 17 criteria in 6 categories, per search result not full text. 344 citations per Heriot-Watt portal (search result).
limits: Abstract only; criteria count is second-hand.
agent_relevance: Another sign there is no single standard method for function decomposition.
